title: Heat In, Heat Out, and the Controller

scenes.visual: Title card: Heat In, Heat Out, and the Controller.

scenes.tts: An animal's body temperature comes down to a balance. Heat made by its own metabolism, plus heat gained from the sun, a rock, air or water, against heat lost to its surroundings. Animals do not just accept that balance. They sense temperature, and a controller adjusts how much heat they make, how much they lose, and what they do. That is how a desert iguana basking on a rock can end up warmer than you are.
scenes.visual: Body box with arrows: heat made (inner metabolism chip), heat gained (sun and rock arrows in), heat lost (arrows out); a gold controller dial appears on the box; then the iguana tag near or above 37 C.

scenes.tts: Heat moves by four routes. Radiation, as when a lizard absorbs sunlight. Conduction, through direct contact, as from a warm rock into its belly. Convection, by moving air or water. And evaporation, as water turns to vapour. The first three run either way. Evaporation only removes heat, and it costs water. Animals adjust these routes with fur and feathers, blood flow to the skin, countercurrent exchange, sweating or panting, and behaviour.
scenes.visual: Body box with four arrows appearing as named; three double-headed, evaporation one-way out; then five dial chips: fur, skin blood flow, countercurrent, sweat or pant, behaviour.

scenes.tts: What adjusts them? In mammals, sensors in the skin report the air around the body, and sensors in the brain, spinal cord and abdomen report the core. A controller in the pre-optic area of the hypothalamus weighs those signals. In the cold, it narrows skin blood vessels and calls for shivering and heat from brown fat. In the warm, it widens skin vessels and turns on sweating or panting. Skin sensors can start this before the core has cooled at all.
scenes.visual: Loop diagram: skin sensor and core sensor boxes feed a gold preoptic controller box; arrows out to cold responses (narrow vessels, shiver, brown fat) and warm responses (widen vessels, sweat or pant); a skin arrow lights first while the core thermometer stays flat.

scenes.tts: Where the heat comes from is a separate question. Mammals and birds are endotherms, warmed mainly by their own metabolism. Ectotherms, like the desert iguana, take their heat mainly from outside, and steer it by moving between sun and shade. Ectotherm names the heat source, not a cold animal.
scenes.visual: Two boxes: endotherm (inner metabolism chip, insulation outline), desert iguana (arrows in from sun and rock, a shade patch it can move to).

scenes.tts: Keeping warm costs energy. Plot an endotherm's resting metabolic rate against air temperature. In the textbook plot, the line is flat inside the thermo-neutral zone, at basal metabolic rate. Below the lower critical temperature, it climbs, as the body makes more heat to match faster loss. The steepness of that climb tracks thermal conductance, how readily heat leaks out. So thick-furred arctic mammals stay flat into much colder air than tropical ones.
scenes.visual: Axes in this sketch; curve drawn: climbs, flat zone, rises; lower and upper critical temperatures marked; a second, shallower curve for thick fur stays flat far further left. No numbers on screen.

scenes.tts: The controller can also move the temperature it defends. In fever, that value is raised, and the body saves heat and makes more to reach it. In torpor, a bird or mammal lowers its temperature and metabolism under control. In hibernating black bears, metabolism fell to about a quarter of basal while body temperature stayed at roughly thirty to thirty-six degrees Celsius. Cooling alone does not explain that. Keep one rule. Heat made and gained equals heat lost, and a controller decides where that balance sits.
scenes.visual: Gold set-point line on a temperature scale rises (fever) and drops (torpor); then bear bars: quarter of basal with temperature band 30 to 36 C; label: cooling alone does not explain; final card repeats heat made plus gained equals heat lost, with the controller dial.
